summary: This standards-track document defines an SDP attribute for negotiating image attributes such as picture size. A small device can say what sizes it can display so the sender doesn't need to scale. This saves memory and processing power on low-end devices.

eli5.summary: A small phone screen can tell the sender what picture size it likes, so the sender sends that size and the phone doesn't have to shrink it.

questions: how to negotiate video resolution in sdp
what is the sdp image attribute
what is sample aspect ratio in sdp
subtitle: An SDP attribute that lets a receiver say which picture sizes it wants, so senders stop wasting bits and receivers stop rescaling.

tldr.problem: A low-end device may have to rescale incoming video, which costs memory and processing power, and a sender that does not know the receiver's preferred size may encode more pixels than are ever displayed.
tldr.mechanism: The media-level SDP attribute imageattr lists acceptable image sizes (x and y ranges, with optional sar, par and q parameters) separately for the send and recv directions, and is negotiated in an offer/answer exchange.
tldr.outcome: The receiver can steer the sender toward the size it actually displays. The RFC covers point-to-point unicast use and notes several awkward interactions with codec parameters.

today: RFC 6236 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the imageattr SDP attribute described in RFC 4566.

sections.title: Why Negotiate Image Size
sections.content:
The RFC defines image size as something that may differ from the physical screen size, for example when video fills only part of a handheld screen and the rest is left for menus. Negotiating it brings several benefits: less distortion from rescaling, lower receiver complexity, optimal quality for the bitrate (a sender need not encode a whole CIF 352x288 image if only 288x256 is shown), predictable memory allocation, and a better aspect ratio choice.

Even where rescaling is not implemented, as in H.264 where it is not mandatory, the attribute tells the encoder which size is preferred and avoids encoding at an unnecessarily large resolution. The RFC also lists reasons to rescale on the sender side, such as camera software already doing zoom and crop.

The scope is point-to-point unicast. Use in centralized conferencing is possible, but the many configuration options make a configuration that suits everyone hard to find.
sections.eli5: If your screen is small, you do not want a giant picture that you have to shrink. It is easier if the sender just makes it the right size to begin with.

sections.title: The imageattr Syntax
sections.content:
imageattr is a media-level SDP attribute defined in ABNF. It names a payload type (PT, or * for all payload types in the media description) followed by up to two directions, send and recv, each with a list of sets or *. Each direction MUST NOT appear more than once. The directions are from the point of view of the sender of the session description. For sendrecv streams both SHOULD be present, and for inactive streams both are RECOMMENDED.

A set looks like [x=...,y=...], where x and y are pixel counts given as a single value, a discrete list, or a range with an optional step such as [320:16:640]. Optional keys, at most one of each per set:

  • sar: the sample aspect ratio (pixel shape). Square pixels give 1.0, and 1.0 is assumed if it is absent.
  • par: the allowed range of picture aspect ratio (x to y), written [min-max].
  • q: preference from 0.0 to 1.0, default 0.5, where higher is preferred.

For sar, an answer MUST NOT include a sar parameter it cannot accept, because including one means it is accepted and removing it means it is not.
sections.eli5: It is a little form with boxes for width and height, plus optional boxes for "how square are the dots" and "how much do you like this size."

sections.title: Offer and Answer Rules
sections.content:
The attribute follows the offer/answer model of RFC 3264. The offerer must support the attributes it offers unless it uses a wildcard. A device with no preference is RECOMMENDED to include a=imageattr:97 send * recv * anyway, so the answerer can state its preferences; wildcards should be replaced by as small a set as possible to avoid uncontrolled message growth.

The answerer may keep the attribute or not, keep some of the offered entries, replace them with a new set (which may cause extra offer/answer exchanges), or drop its send direction entirely. It should not add the attribute if the offer lacked it.

If the answer has no imageattr, the offerer SHOULD proceed as if it had not been offered. If the answer has it but nothing is usable, the offerer MUST find another way to choose a size and must issue a new offer/answer without the attribute, which avoids infinite negotiation.

If the answerer uses a different payload type number than the offer, the attribute MUST be split in two in the answer, one line for the send part under the offer's number and one for the recv part under the answer's number. The wildcard alternatives MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: One side lists the sizes it likes, the other crosses out the ones it cannot do and sends the list back. If nothing works, they go back to guessing and start over politely.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the high-level example, Alice offers a send list and either a desired recv list or *, which asks Bob to list the sizes he can send. If Bob supports nothing in one direction, that part is removed from the answer.

Example 1 offers two sizes for sending, 800x640 with sar=1.1 and q=0.6, and 480x320, and asks to receive 330x250. If Bob cannot send 330x250 he replies with a list of acceptable x and y ranges, Alice picks the closest valid size (336x256), and a second offer/answer settles it.

Example 3 combines imageattr with an H.264 fmtp line whose sprop-parameter-sets describes 320x240. The answer picks 320x240 both ways, so no extra exchange is needed, and it splits the attribute because the payload type changes from 99 to 100.

Example 4 shows sar compensation. Alice asks to receive 800x600 with sar=1.1, so a sender with square pixels would rescale an 880x600 image to 800x600.
sections.eli5: The examples show two people trading offers like a menu: "I can do these sizes," "I will take this one," and sometimes one more round to agree.

sections.title: Interaction with Codec Parameters
sections.content:
Many codecs already state image size on the fmtp line, which can conflict with imageattr. H.263 (RFC 4629) lists image sizes that the answerer cannot modify. H.264 (RFC 6184) uses sprop-parameter-sets, which is not a negotiation, though it can be changed inband later. MPEG-4 (RFC 3016) uses a config parameter that cannot be changed inband.

The RFC lists possible solutions without recommending one: ignore the payload format parameters, run a second session-wide offer/answer, or run a second round only for video with the port set to zero in the first round, which can delay video by up to 2 seconds.

Other considerations: asymmetric sizes are limited by codec profile levels, since the same level applies in both directions (H.264 solves this with level-asymmetry-allowed); renegotiating image size is RECOMMENDED when a user changes display mid-call; for layered codecs the same attribute should go on each media description or only on the base layer; and unknown future parameters MUST be ignored and not echoed in the answer.
sections.eli5: Some video formats already announce a picture size in their own way. The two announcements must agree, and the RFC lists a few ways to keep them from fighting.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Image size values can cause memory or CPU exhaustion, through a mistake or an attack by a malicious SDP sender, in the same way as extreme values on an a=fmtp line. A receiver MUST make sure the values are reasonable and manageable for the device.

Simple parameter checks may not catch every Denial-of-Service problem for some SDPs and deployments, so implementers ought to consider whether other DoS attacks exist.
sections.eli5: Someone could ask for an absurdly huge picture to overload a phone. So the phone should check that the request is sensible before agreeing.

messages.label: Offer: send 800x640 or 480x320, recv 330x250
messages.note: The 800x640 set has sar=1.1 and q=0.6.

messages.label: Answer: lists sizes he can send
messages.note: 330x250 is not supported, so Bob offers x and y ranges.

messages.label: Second offer: recv 336x256
messages.note: Alice picks the closest valid size to the one she wanted.
